stimulus.markdown:
Economists have long treated their instruments as mirrors: a price index reflects inflation, an unemployment rate reflects idleness, a credit score reflects the risk that a borrower will default. The metaphor is convenient and, within limits, harmless. It becomes misleading the moment a measure acquires an audience. Once a credit score governs access to a mortgage, borrowers begin to manage the score rather than the prudence it was built to detect; lenders, in turn, price loans off the managed score. What began as a description of behaviour becomes one of the pressures that shape it. The measure is not merely inaccurate; it is productive.

It is tempting to read this as an indictment of quantification, and some critics do. The inference is too quick. Nothing in the argument shows that unmeasured judgment is more faithful to the world; loan officers working on intuition were biased in ways no one audited, and their errors, being invisible, were also uncorrectable. What the argument establishes is narrower and more awkward: the accuracy of a social measure is not a fixed property of the measure but a function of how consequential it has been allowed to become. A statistic used only by researchers may describe reasonably well what it claims to describe. The same statistic, once written into a contract or a regulation, begins to erode its own validity, and does so at a rate that has little to do with the care taken in its construction.

This has an uncomfortable corollary for institutional design. If validity decays with use, then the standard remedy, refining the metric, addresses the wrong variable. Better specification may buy time; it cannot arrest the process, because the process is driven not by measurement error but by the incentives that consequence creates. The alternatives are unattractive in different ways: rotate metrics before they are gamed, and lose comparability across periods; keep several imperfect indicators in play, and abandon the crisp accountability a single number provides; or make the metric one input among several to a judgment that remains discretionary, and therefore hard to challenge. None of these is a solution. Each is a choice about which kind of failure a system prefers to live with.

question_text: **The passage is primarily concerned with establishing which of the following?**

options.1: Credit scoring shows how a poorly constructed statistic can end up distorting the very market that comes to depend on it.
options.2: Because quantitative indicators are routinely gamed, consequential decisions are better left to experienced human judgment.
options.3: Social measures fail chiefly because those who design them pay too little attention to how the underlying quantity is defined.
options.4: A measure's validity falls once it is given consequences, so refining its design cannot fix the problem.

explanation: The passage argues that accuracy is a function of how consequential a measure has been allowed to become, and that refining the metric addresses the wrong variable. The appeal to human judgment is blocked by the paragraph on unaudited loan officers. Credit scoring is one illustration, not the thesis, and the passage explicitly says decay has little to do with care in construction.

stimulus.markdown:
Reformers who export institutions tend to work from a plausible premise: if a commercial code, a bankruptcy statute or a securities regulator produced prosperity in one place, the same text should help elsewhere. The record is not encouraging. Codes copied faithfully have been ignored, applied selectively, or absorbed into arrangements their drafters never imagined. The usual explanation is cultural: rules that suit one society's habits will not suit another's. That explanation is loose enough to accommodate any outcome, which is a reason to distrust it rather than a reason to accept it.

A tighter account starts from what a rule is for. A rule does useful work only when parties can predict how others, including officials, will respond to its breach. That prediction rests on a stock of shared expectation built up through repeated enforcement, and such a stock cannot be imported, because it is not contained in the text. A transplanted rule therefore arrives without the very thing that made it effective at home. Whether it acquires one depends less on the fit between the rule and local values than on whether somebody with something to lose finds it worth invoking, repeatedly, before officials who face some cost for ignoring it.

This reframing has consequences. It predicts that transplants will take hold in narrow commercial domains, where a few well resourced parties litigate often, before they take hold in areas of diffuse benefit, where no single stake is large enough to sustain the litigation that generates expectation. It also predicts that the most durable transplants may be the least faithful: rules bent to serve interests that already existed get enforced, while pristine copies gather dust. Reformers who measure success by fidelity to the model will therefore misread their own results, treating as failure the drift that is the mechanism of adoption.

None of this restores the reformers' optimism; it relocates the difficulty. The obstacle is not that societies are incompatible with foreign rules, but that the asset which makes rules work is produced slowly, locally, and only as a by-product of use. Where no one uses a rule, no argument about its merits will make it operative.

question_text: **Which of the following comes closest to the claim the passage is defending?**

options.1: Reform programmes that export commercial codes to other jurisdictions should be discontinued as a matter of policy.
options.2: Bankruptcy statutes and securities regulation are the two bodies of law least suited to transfer across borders.
options.3: Transplants stall less from cultural mismatch than from missing shared expectation, which only local use builds.
options.4: Legal transplants take root only in those societies that already share the values held by the exporting country.

explanation: The second and fourth paragraphs make the stock of shared expectation, which cannot travel in a text, the binding constraint, and expressly downgrade fit with local values. Requiring shared values reverses that; abandoning reform is never recommended, since the author only relocates the difficulty; and the named statutes are examples rather than a ranking.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be arranged to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not belong.

(1) Every map begins with an act of omission, since a representation that kept all the detail of a place would be as unusable as the place itself.
(2) The cartographer must therefore decide in advance which features a reader will need and which can be silently discarded.
(3) Recent surveys report that most commuters now consult digital route planners rather than printed atlases.
(4) Those early decisions harden over time into conventions, and later users mistake the conventions for properties of the world.
(5) What looks like a neutral record of terrain is thus the residue of a long series of judgements about relevance.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 4 and 5 build one argument: maps must omit, so a cartographer selects, the selections become conventions, and the finished map is therefore a record of judgements about relevance. Sentence 3 makes an empirical claim about which media commuters use today, which contributes nothing to the argument about selection and is the misfit. Sentence 1 is the natural opener, 2 follows from it through therefore, and 5 is the closing generalisation, so none of those can be removed without breaking the chain.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be arranged to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not belong.

(1) Experts seldom deliberate over the moves that most impress onlookers; they recognise a familiar pattern and act before reasons are available to them.
(2) Such fluency is bought by long exposure to situations that return prompt and unambiguous feedback.
(3) Where the feedback is delayed or noisy, however, long experience yields confidence without yielding accuracy.
(4) Novices, by contrast, report that they enjoy the earliest stages of learning a craft far more than the later ones.
(5) Intuition therefore deserves trust only after one has asked what the environment has actually been teaching.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 form a single line of reasoning about when expert intuition can be trusted: it looks effortless, it depends on good feedback, it fails where feedback is poor, and the practical rule follows. Sentence 4 reports how much novices enjoy learning, a claim about affect rather than about the reliability of intuition, so it is the outsider. Sentence 3 cannot be the answer because however marks exactly the contrast that sentence 5 then resolves.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be arranged to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not belong.

(1) A quantity chosen to stand for a goal starts to be pursued for its own sake as soon as rewards are attached to it.
(2) Staff learn quickly which parts of their work are counted, and effort drains away from everything that is not.
(3) The published figures then improve while the purpose they were meant to serve quietly deteriorates.
(4) Organisations often adopt measurement schemes less to inform their own decisions than to demonstrate propriety to outside audiences.
(5) Auditors, reading only the figures, record success and recommend that the scheme be extended to further departments.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 trace one causal sequence: attaching rewards to an indicator redirects effort, the indicator rises as the underlying purpose decays, and auditors who see only the indicator extend the scheme. Sentence 4 stays on the same subject but shifts the level of analysis, explaining why organisations take up measurement at all rather than what measurement does to behaviour, and it plays no part in the causal chain. Sentence 5 belongs because it supplies the consequence of the improved figures named in sentence 3.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below, labelled 1 to 5. Four of them can be arranged to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not belong.

(1) No translator can carry every feature of a sentence across, so the work consists largely in deciding what to give up.
(2) Readers tend to praise the translations that read most smoothly and to distrust those that preserve the strangeness of the original.
(3) A pun that depends on sound may be replaced by one that depends on sense, on the ground that the joke matters more than its mechanism.
(4) Rhythm surrendered in one line is sometimes repaid in another, the debt being settled across the page rather than within it.
(5) Every such compensation is an argument about which layer of the original counts as the text itself.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 3, 4 and 5 describe the translator's own practice: loss is unavoidable, so features are traded and debts are repaid elsewhere, and each trade amounts to a claim about what the text essentially is. Sentence 2 describes how readers receive finished translations, a claim about reception rather than about the decisions being made, and the paragraph neveruses it. Sentence 4 is not the misfit because the repayment it describes is one instance of the compensation that sentence 5 generalises.

question_text:
The four sentences below, labelled 1 to 4, are not in order. Arrange them into a logical paragraph.

(1) That demand is what makes boredom productive, since it pushes the mind to supply what the surroundings withhold.
(2) Boredom is usually described as an absence, the gap left when nothing outside us claims our attention.
(3) But the state has a content of its own, a restless demand that the world become more interesting than it is.
(4) Children left with nothing to do therefore stay idle only briefly, building a game out of whatever lies nearest.

**Which of the following is the correct order of the sentences?**
explanation: Sentence 2 gives the standard description and must open. Sentence 3 begins with But and corrects that description by introducing the restless demand. Sentence 1 picks that demand up with That demand, so it can only follow. Sentence 4 closes with therefore and an illustration. The order beginning 2134 fails because That demand has no antecedent yet, 3241 puts the correction before what it corrects, and 2341 leaves sentence 1 stranded after the example it explains.

question_text:
The four sentences below, labelled 1 to 4, are not in order. Arrange them into a logical paragraph.

(1) Once the date is fixed, the remaining hours acquire a rank, and the work is fitted to those that are left.
(2) This is why arbitrary dates can serve as well as reasoned ones, provided they are actually believed.
(3) A deadline works less by adding motivation than by removing alternatives.
(4) Until a date is fixed, every hour is a candidate for the task and no hour is obliged to be.

**Which of the following is the correct order of the sentences?**
explanation: Sentence 3 states the thesis about removing alternatives and opens. Sentences 4 and 1 form the matched pair Until a date is fixed and Once the date is fixed, in that order, since the second echoes the first. Sentence 2 draws the inference with This is why and must end. The order 3142 breaks the Until and Once pair, 4312 buries the thesis, and 3421 places the inference before the mechanism it depends on.

question_text:
The four sentences below, labelled 1 to 4, are not in order. Arrange them into a logical paragraph.

(1) The only reliable lever, then, is conduct that gives those custodians something else to carry.
(2) Its custodians are third parties, who pass it on for reasons of their own and revise it without notice.
(3) Reputation is information about us that we do not own and cannot directly edit.
(4) This dependence explains why attempts at correction so often deepen the damage, for a correction is itself testimony and it travels.

**Which of the following is the correct order of the sentences?**
explanation: Only sentence 3 introduces reputation as a full noun, so the pronoun Its in sentence 2 must come after it. Sentence 4 opens with This dependence, which refers to the reliance on third parties just established, and sentence 1 closes with then and with those custodians. The order 2341 and 2431 both strand the pronoun Its ahead of its antecedent, and 3421 makes This dependence point at nothing but the definition.

question_text:
The four sentences below, labelled 1 to 4, are not in order. Arrange them into a logical paragraph.

(1) A first reading of anything difficult is mostly navigation, since we are still learning where the parts are.
(2) Readers who skip it are not saving time; they are trading comprehension for the feeling of having finished.
(3) For this reason a second reading is not a repetition but a different task, undertaken with the map the first reading drew.
(4) Only once the shape is known can attention be spent on the joints, which is where arguments usually fail.

**Which of the following is the correct order of the sentences?**

question_text:
Infrastructure is noticed chiefly when it fails. A water main, a switching station, a clearing house: each is built to disappear into the routines it supports, and its success is measured by how little thought it demands. The consequence is political rather than technical. Systems nobody thinks about attract neither scrutiny nor investment, and their upkeep competes badly with projects that can be photographed. Failure then arrives as a surprise, and the surprise is used to argue that nobody could have foreseen it.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Public money should be redirected from photogenic new construction towards the unglamorous upkeep of water mains, switching stations and clearing houses.
options.2: Infrastructure fails because engineers deliberately design systems to disappear, and systems that are invisible are inherently more fragile than visible ones.
options.3: Since infrastructure failures are always surprises, the political value of such systems lies in the attention that their breakdowns finally bring to them.
options.4: Designed to go unnoticed, working infrastructure draws little scrutiny or funding, so its breakdowns look unforeseeable when they were merely unattended.

question_text:
Averaging many independent guesses often beats the best single guess, because errors pointing in opposite directions cancel. The condition doing the work is independence. Once the guessers can hear one another, their errors begin to align, and the average inherits a bias instead of shedding one. Committees that deliberate before voting therefore give up much of the advantage voting was supposed to secure, and the confidence produced by agreement rises just as the accuracy it is taken to signal falls.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Confidence is a poor guide to accuracy, since agreement inside a group can show only that its members have all been exposed to the same limited information.
options.2: Groups outperform their ablest members because pooling opinions cancels error, which is why committees ought always to vote instead of trusting one expert.
options.3: Aggregation improves accuracy only while guesses stay independent; discussion correlates errors, so deliberating groups gain confidence and lose accuracy.
options.4: Deliberation harms committees chiefly because the members who happen to speak first impose their own private biases on all of those who speak later.

explanation: The paragraph makes independence the load-bearing condition and ends on the divergence between rising confidence and falling accuracy, which the summary naming both captures. question_text:
Options are usually treated as free, on the view that holding one costs nothing until it is exercised. In practice every open possibility levies a quiet charge: some attention reserved, some commitment withheld, some relationship kept provisional. Because the charge is never invoiced, options accumulate well past the point where their combined upkeep exceeds anything they could deliver. The person who cannot choose is not made richer by the alternatives; the alternatives are consuming the very capacity that choosing would have released.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Open possibilities exact hidden upkeep in attention and commitment, so options collected beyond a point cost more than they could ever deliver.
options.2: Because an option costs nothing at all until it is exercised, a rational person should hold as many as possible and delay commitment for as long as possible.
options.3: Indecisive people are poorer than decisive ones, because real wealth consists in commitments actually made rather than in alternatives that remain available.
options.4: The chief trouble with unexercised options is that their true price is never invoiced, which makes any accounting of their value unreliable in practice.

explanation: The paragraph identifies a hidden cost of holding options and locates a threshold past which the cost outweighs the benefit, which the summary about upkeep exceeding delivery states. The advice to hold as many options as possible repeats the view the paragraph is arguing against. The claim about indecisive people being poorer generalises into a thesis about wealth that the text does not assert. The uninvoiced price is only the reason the cost goes unnoticed, not the main point.

question_text:
Forecasts about human affairs are not merely difficult; they are ingredients. A published prediction of shortage produces hoarding, and a published prediction of stability invites the risk-taking that ends it. This does not make forecasting useless, but it changes what accuracy could mean, since a forecast can be judged only against the world it helped to make, and a forecast that is widely ignored may be the only one ever fairly tested. Practitioners who forget this treat their failures as errors of measurement and answer them by refining instruments that were never the problem.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Predictions about human affairs are self-fulfilling, so forecasters should publish nothing until their instruments are accurate enough to withstand contact with the public.
options.2: Predictions about human affairs alter the conditions they describe, so accuracy can be judged only against an already altered world, and better instruments cannot help.
options.3: Social forecasts change the behaviour they describe, which is why only those forecasts that nobody happens to notice can ever be tested fairly against events.
options.4: Failures of social forecasting come from measurement error, and sharper instruments will in time let practitioners predict hoarding and risk-taking reliably enough.

explanation: The paragraph's main claim is that because forecasts feed back into events, accuracy must be redefined and better instruments cannot rescue the enterprise, which is the summary mentioning both the altered world and the instruments. The version about forecasts nobody notices repeats a subordinate aside and leaves out the conclusion about measurement. The advice to publish nothing adds a prescription and treats every forecast as self-fulfilling, which the shortage and stability cases contradict. Blaming measurement error states the mistake the paragraph diagnoses.

question_text:
A standard is valuable in proportion to how many people already use it, so its merits and its market share are hard to tell apart. Once adoption passes a threshold, the standard is defended by everything built on top of it, and a technically superior rival must compensate not for a small gap in quality but for the whole accumulated weight of compatibility. Arguments about which standard is better therefore arrive too late to matter, and the winner's supporters read its survival as evidence that the argument was settled on the merits.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Technically superior standards displace entrenched ones eventually, provided their supporters can show that the original choice was never really settled on the merits.
options.2: A standard's worth grows with its user base, so entrenched standards defeat better rivals through compatibility, and survival is then misread as proof of merit.
options.3: Because compatibility counts for more than quality, users should simply adopt whichever standard is most widely used instead of assessing competing designs themselves.
options.4: A standard's dominance owes far more to the number of people using it than to its quality, so late arguments about technical merit rarely change which one prevails.

explanation: The paragraph moves from network value to compatibility lock-out and ends with the mistaken inference from survival to superiority, all three of which the summary about misread survival preserves. The version about late arguments is accurate as far as it goes but stops before that inference, which is the paragraph's sting. The claim that superior standards eventually win reverses the argument. The advice to adopt the most popular standard converts a diagnosis into guidance the text does not offer.

question_text:
An archive looks like a residue of the past, but it is a residue of past decisions about what would be worth keeping. Records survive because someone was obliged to file them, and the obligations fell unevenly, heavily on property and litigation and hardly at all on ordinary agreement. Historians who read the surviving mass as a sample of what happened therefore reconstruct a world of disputes and transactions and miss the settled life around them. The remedy is not more documents but a habit of asking, of every silence, whether it records an absence or only an exemption from paperwork.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Because filing obligations bore most heavily on property and litigation, surviving archives over-represent disputes and transactions at the expense of ordinary agreement.
options.2: Every silence in an archive records a genuine absence, which is why the past appears to consist mainly of litigation, transactions and disputes rather than agreement.
options.3: Historians ought to seek out further documents about settled everyday life, since the archives that do survive were shaped by the interests of owners and courts.
options.4: Archives keep whatever filing duties happened to capture, so reading them as a fair sample distorts the past unless each silence is itself interrogated.

explanation: The paragraph diagnoses a bias created by uneven filing duties and then prescribes a way of reading silences, and only the summary combining distortion with interrogating silences carries both halves. The statement about property and litigation is true but stops at the diagnosis and omits the remedy. The suggestion to seek more documents is precisely the remedy the text rules out. The assertion that every silence records a real absence states the error the paragraph warns against.

stimulus.markdown:
When we ask what a poem means, we are tempted to reach for what its author intended it to mean, as though the work were a sealed letter and criticism the act of opening it. The temptation is understandable, since intentions do govern most of what we make and say. Yet a strand of twentieth-century criticism insisted that, once a work is finished and released, the author's private aims cease to be the arbiter of its meaning. On this view the poem is a public object made of language, and language carries implications its user may neither have foreseen nor endorsed. A reader who recovers a documented intention has learned something about the poet's biography, not necessarily something decisive about the poem.

The argument is easy to caricature as a licence for arbitrary reading, but its careful proponents claimed no such thing. They distinguished the meaning of a work from the occasion of its composition, and held that evidence internal to the text, its diction, structure, and the conventions it invokes, constrains interpretation more tightly than any appeal to what the author confided in a letter. Where internal and external evidence agree, the appeal to intention is redundant; where they conflict, it is the text, not the confession, that the critic is professionally bound to honour. Intention, in short, is neither available nor desirable as a final standard of literary judgement.

Critics of this position have replied that meaning without a meaner is incoherent, and that to strip intention from interpretation is to reduce reading to the free play of association. The reply has force against the caricature but less against the original claim, which never denied that someone meant something, only that the someone's report settles the question. A more searching objection notes that the very conventions the text invokes are themselves the sediment of countless past intentions, so that intention returns, collectivised, at the level of the language itself. The debate, then, is less about whether intention matters than about whose intention, and at what remove, a competent reading is obliged to reconstruct.

question_text: **The passage is primarily concerned with:**

options.1: defending the claim that a reader is free to assign a poem almost any meaning that the language will loosely permit
options.2: tracing how twentieth-century literary criticism gradually abandoned nearly all close attention to the words on the page
options.3: presenting a view that denies the author's intention fixes a poem's meaning, and weighing the replies it draws
options.4: arguing that an author's stated intention is wholly irrelevant to every form of literary and biographical inquiry

explanation: The passage lays out the anti-intention position (paragraphs 1 to 2) and then the objections to it (paragraph 3), ending on what the dispute is really about. It does not claim intention is irrelevant everywhere; it grants intention is biographically informative and even returns collectivised, so the 'wholly irrelevant' option overstates. The 'any meaning' option is the caricature the passage explicitly rejects. The historical-abandonment option is a scope shift the text never makes.

stimulus.markdown:
For a generation, the standard verdict on shared resources was pessimistic: where no one owns a pasture, a fishery, or an aquifer, each user has an incentive to take as much as possible before a rival does, and the resource is ruined by the sum of individually rational choices. The remedy seemed to follow with the force of a theorem. Either the state must regulate the resource from above, or it must be carved into private parcels whose owners will husband what they hold. Between the regulator and the auctioneer there appeared to be no third path.

Field research complicated the theorem. In mountain villages, coastal fisheries, and irrigation systems that had endured for centuries, users had neither nationalised nor privatised their commons, yet had not destroyed them either. Instead they had crafted their own rules: who could harvest, when, how much, and what would befall a cheat. These arrangements were neither spontaneous nor costless. They depended on the users being able to monitor one another, to communicate, to revise the rules as conditions changed, and to impose graduated penalties that punished a first offence lightly and a repeated one severely. Where such conditions were absent, the pessimistic prediction often held.

The lesson was not that the original model was false, but that it described one case rather than the general one. The model assumed users who could not talk, could not watch, and could not bind themselves, and for such users the grim conclusion does follow. Real communities are frequently able to do all three, and the capacity to make and enforce local agreements is itself a resource, one that erodes if outsiders, however well intentioned, override it. A government that replaces a working local arrangement with a uniform national rule may extinguish the very monitoring and trust on which restraint depended, and so produce the tragedy it meant to prevent.

question_text: **Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?**

options.1: Communities can sometimes govern shared resources by self-made rules, so the pessimistic model fits a special case
options.2: State regulation from above is shown to be the single most dependable remedy for the overuse of any common resource
options.3: Traditional rural communities, unlike modern states, essentially never deplete the natural resources placed in their care
options.4: Shared resources are inevitably destroyed unless they are divided up into privately owned parcels by their own users

explanation: The passage argues the grim model holds only for users who cannot monitor, communicate, or bind themselves, while many real communities can and so govern their commons without nationalising or privatising them. The privatisation-inevitable and regulation-most-dependable options each pick one of the two paths the passage relativises. The 'never deplete' option overstates: the text says the prediction 'often held' where the enabling conditions were absent.

Real communities are frequently able to do all three, and the capacity to make and enforce local agreements is itself a resource, one that erodes if outsiders, however well intentioned, override it. A government that replaces a working local arrangement with a uniform national rule may extinguish the very monitoring and trust on which restraint depended, and so produce the tragedy it meant to prevent.

question_text: **The author's stance toward the original pessimistic model is best described as:**

options.1: full endorsement of it as a fixed law that governs shared resources in every setting
options.2: studied indifference, on the ground that the model's assumptions are said to be untestable
options.3: outright rejection of it as an account that field evidence has now proved plainly false
options.4: qualified acceptance, treating it as accurate for a restricted range of conditions

explanation: The author says explicitly the lesson is 'not that the original model was false' but that it fits one case, and that for users who cannot talk, watch, or bind themselves 'the grim conclusion does follow'. That is qualified acceptance. Outright rejection contradicts the disclaimer; full endorsement ignores the restriction to a special case; indifference is wrong because the model is engaged with closely and its assumptions are tested against field cases.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below. Four of them combine to form a single coherent paragraph; one does not belong. Read the sentences and identify the misfit.

(1) A tidal wetland acts as a natural buffer, absorbing the energy of incoming storm surges before they reach inland settlements.
(2) Its dense mat of roots binds loose sediment, so the shoreline erodes far more slowly than an unvegetated coast would.
(3) The same roots filter runoff, trapping pollutants that would otherwise flow straight into open water.
(4) Because of these functions, planners increasingly treat wetlands as infrastructure rather than as idle land.
(5) Modern desalination plants can convert seawater into drinking water at a steadily falling cost per litre.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 4 build one argument: wetlands buffer surges, hold sediment, filter runoff, and so count as infrastructure. The desalination-plant sentence introduces an unrelated technology for producing drinking water and shares none of that thread, so it is the intruder. Sentence 4 begins with 'these functions', which points back to the wetland benefits, confirming the other four cohere.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below. Four of them combine to form a single coherent paragraph; one does not belong. Read the sentences and identify the misfit.

(1) When a folk tale passes from one teller to the next, small changes creep in with every retelling.
(2) A teller may drop a name, sharpen a joke, or shift the setting to a place the listeners know.
(3) Over generations these tiny edits accumulate into strikingly different versions of one story.
(4) Scholars can sometimes trace those versions back to a shared ancestor by comparing their fixed motifs.
(5) Printing presses lowered the price of books so sharply that private libraries became common.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: The four connected sentences describe how oral folk tales mutate as they are retold and how scholars reconstruct their common origin. The sentence about printing presses and the price of books concerns written distribution, a different subject that breaks the chain about oral transmission, making it the misfit. The word 'those versions' in sentence 4 links back to the accumulated edits, tying the other four together.

question_text:
Five sentences are given below. Four of them combine to form a single coherent paragraph; one does not belong. Read the sentences and identify the misfit.

(1) A scientific model is deliberately simpler than the reality it represents, keeping only the features that matter for a given question.
(2) By stripping away detail, it lets researchers reason about a system that would otherwise be too tangled to follow.
(3) The value of a model therefore lies not in its completeness but in the useful predictions it yields.
(4) A model that reproduced every detail of the world would be as hard to understand as the world itself.
(5) A well-designed model can be tested against fresh observations and discarded the moment it fails to predict them.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 4 develop one idea, that a model earns its worth through simplification rather than through completeness. Sentence 5 is subtly off: it stays on the topic of models but shifts to a different claim, about falsification and testing against new data, which the other four never raise. Because 5 introduces a separate virtue instead of extending the completeness-versus-usefulness argument, it is the odd one out.

Five sentences are given below. Four of them combine to form a single coherent paragraph; one does not belong. Read the sentences and identify the misfit.

(1) A currency holds its value only because the people using it expect others to accept it tomorrow.
(2) That expectation is a shared belief, sustained by habit and by trust in the issuing authority.
(3) When the belief weakens, holders rush to spend, and prices climb faster than the notes can be printed.
(4) A sudden loss of confidence can thus unravel a currency long before any change in the goods it can buy.
(5) Central banks set interest rates to steer how much borrowing and lending take place across the economy.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: The cohering four trace one causal story: a currency's value rests on shared expectation, that expectation is belief, weakened belief triggers a spending rush, and confidence can collapse before real goods change. Sentence 5 also concerns central banking but makes a different claim, about interest-rate policy and credit, rather than the psychology of confidence. It sits in the same field yet breaks the single argument, so it is the intruder.

3. This stored fat becomes the fuel that powers days of almost continuous flight.
4. Without it, a small migrant could not cross the wide deserts and seas that lie along the route.

**Select the correct order.**
explanation: Sentence 1 sets the scene with the autumn departure and is the natural opener. Sentence 2 explains the preparation, doubling body weight, which sentence 3 then labels 'this stored fat' and calls the fuel. **Select the correct order.**
explanation: The paragraph moves through time. Sentence 1 gives the humble origin, a donated room. The four sentences below, labelled 1 to 4, have been jumbled. Arrange them to form a coherent paragraph.

4. History, they argued, rarely rewards those who mistake a rough prototype for a finished tool.

**Select the correct order.**
explanation: Sentence 1 states the dismissal and must open. Sentence 2 begins 'Its defenders replied', a direct rebuttal that has to follow the criticism. 4. For this reason a map is best read not only as a guide but as an argument about what deserves notice.

**Select the correct order.**

question_text:
Many species that appear wasteful are in fact insuring themselves against bad years. An oak may drop thousands of acorns although only a handful can ever grow into trees, because the surplus swamps the animals that eat them and guarantees that a few seeds survive in almost any season. What looks like extravagance is a hedge: by producing far more than the average conditions require, the tree buys protection against the years when conditions are worst.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Apparent overproduction in nature is often a safeguard, letting a species survive poor years by making far more offspring than good conditions alone would need.
options.2: Animals that feed on seeds are usually overwhelmed by the sheer number a plant produces and so fail to eat the entire crop.
options.3: Oak trees drop many thousands of acorns every single year even though almost none of those scattered acorns will ever manage to grow into a mature standing tree.
options.4: Nature tends to be wasteful, and much of what living things produce serves no real purpose beyond simple excess.

explanation: The passage argues that seeming waste is really insurance against bad years, using the oak only as an example. The correct summary captures that general point about overproduction as a safeguard. The acorn statement and the seed-eater statement are single supporting details, too narrow to be the summary, and the 'nature is wasteful' option flatly contradicts the passage, which says the surplus has a clear purpose.

question_text:
A new road built to relieve congestion often ends up just as crowded as before. The extra capacity lowers the effective cost of driving, so people who once avoided the trip, took the train, or travelled at odd hours now join the traffic. Within a few years the freed-up space fills again, and the promised relief quietly disappears even though the road itself was built exactly as planned.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Roads are frequently built exactly to their original plans, yet the traffic engineers still misjudge how drivers will respond.
options.2: Adding road capacity tends to attract new trips that fill the space, so the expected easing of congestion often fails to last.
options.3: Traffic congestion is one of the most stubborn and expensive problems that fast-growing modern cities are forced to confront.
options.4: People who used to take the train will switch to driving as soon as a wider and more convenient road becomes available to them.

explanation: The paragraph's core claim is that new capacity induces extra demand that refills the road, defeating the intended relief. The correct option states exactly that cause and effect. The train-switching option is only one instance of the induced demand, the 'built to plan' option seizes a side remark, and the 'congestion is stubborn' option is a general theme the passage never actually argues.

question_text:
Learning a second language as an adult rarely produces a flawless accent, yet the effort is far from wasted. Even partial fluency reshapes how the learner hears speech, sharpens attention to grammar in the first language, and opens doors to texts and people that were closed before. The goal need not be to pass as a native; the practical and mental gains arrive long before that distant point.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: Studying grammar in a new language happens to sharpen a learner's awareness of the grammar of their own first language.
options.2: Reaching the fluent level of a genuine native speaker is really the one true and proper measure of success for anyone setting out to learn a new foreign language.
options.3: Adult language learning brings real practical and mental benefits well before fluency, so a perfect accent need not be the aim.
options.4: Adults who study a second language almost never manage to acquire an accent that a native speaker would accept as flawless.

explanation: The passage says adult learners seldom sound native but gain much sooner, so a perfect accent is not the point. The correct summary states both halves, benefits arrive early and native-level need not be the goal. The accent option and the grammar option are isolated details, and the 'native speaker is the true measure' option reverses the passage's actual conclusion.

question_text:
Rating systems promise to guide us toward quality, but a high average can mislead as easily as it informs. A product reviewed by only a dozen buyers may score higher than a rival reviewed by thousands, not because it is better but because a small sample swings more wildly. Worse, the people who bother to rate are rarely typical: the delighted and the furious speak up while the merely satisfied stay silent. A score, then, summarises not the product alone but the peculiar crowd that chose to judge it, and reading it wisely means asking who did the rating before trusting what they said.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: A product judged by only a handful of reviewers can post a higher average than a rival that thousands of buyers have carefully rated.
options.2: Rating systems were originally designed to steer ordinary shoppers toward higher quality goods, and for the most part they seem to carry out that useful task quite reliably.
options.3: People who feel delighted or furious about a purchase are much more likely to leave a review than those who feel merely satisfied.
options.4: Average ratings can mislead because small samples fluctuate and reviewers are unrepresentative, so a score reflects who rated as much as the product.

explanation: The passage makes two linked points, that small samples swing and that reviewers are a skewed crowd, concluding a score reflects its raters. Only the correct option carries that full scope. The small-sample option and the delighted-or-furious option are each one of the two reasons, true but partial, and the reliability option contradicts the passage by calling ratings reliable, which is the very claim being questioned.

question_text:
We tend to praise the lone inventor, but most breakthroughs are less a single leap than a last step. By the time a discovery is announced, dozens of others have usually reached the same threshold, held back only by a missing tool or an unasked question. The celebrated name is often simply the one who arrived days ahead, or who framed the result in words the age was ready to hear. To credit a single mind, then, is to mistake the visible tip of a long collective effort for the whole of it.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.1: The lone individual inventor still fully deserves the praise that we give, because framing a raw result in exactly the right words is itself the single hardest part of any discovery.
options.2: Great discoveries are usually the final step of a wide shared effort, so crediting one inventor mistakes a visible moment for the whole.
options.3: A breakthrough is frequently delayed by nothing more than a missing instrument or a question that no one has yet thought to ask.
options.4: Whoever announces a discovery first has often arrived only a few days ahead of several rivals working on the very same problem.

explanation: The passage argues that breakthroughs cap a broad collective effort and that honouring one mind mistakes the tip for the whole. The correct option states both the shared-effort claim and its consequence. The 'arrived days ahead' and 'missing instrument' options are supporting details, and the final option endorses the lone-inventor view the passage sets out to overturn.

The damage lies less in the single ignored statute than in the lesson it spreads about how seriously any law should be taken.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

options.2: An unenforced law erodes respect for law in general, because tolerating its breach teaches that rules need not be obeyed.
options.3: Lawmakers should take care to repeal statutes they no longer intend to enforce rather than leaving them on the books.
options.4: A rule that stays on the books without ever being enforced does not vanish but quietly remains available for later use.

explanation: The passage's thesis is that an ignored law spreads a corrosive lesson, weakening obedience to law as a whole. The correct option captures that broad erosion and its cause. The 'remains available' option distorts a minor phrase, the 'next violation easier' option is one step in the argument rather than the whole, and the repeal recommendation is advice the passage never offers.

explanation: The vessel holds 42 litres of milk and 18 litres of water. Milk does not change, so for the ratio 7 : 5 the water must become 42 x 5 / 7 = 30 litres, needing 30 - 18 = 12 litres more. The 10 litres value comes from wrongly making total volume 70. The 15 litres value comes from taking the new water as one quarter of a 60 litre base. The 8 litres value comes from using the ratio difference 5 - 3 = 2 on 4 litre parts.

verification.expr: milk = 60 * 7 / 10; water = 60 * 3 / 10; x = milk * 5 / 7 - water; '2' if abs(x - 12) < 1e-9 else '0'

question_text: A motorboat whose speed in still water is 12 km/h goes 45 km downstream along a river and returns to the starting point, taking 8 hours in all. What is the speed of the current?
explanation: If the current is s, then 45 / (12 + s) + 45 / (12 - s) = 8, so 45 x 24 = 8 x (144 - s squared), giving 144 - s squared = 135 and s = 3 km/h. The 4 km/h value comes from averaging the two legs at 45 / 4 hours each. The 2.5 km/h value comes from solving with a total of 7.5 hours. The 6 km/h value comes from equating the round trip to a single 90 km run at 12 - s.

question_text: Anil alone can paint a hall in 20 days and Bimal alone can paint it in 30 days. They begin painting together, but Anil stops working 5 days before the hall is finished, and Bimal completes the remaining part alone. In how many days is the hall painted?
explanation: If the job takes T days, Bimal works all T days and Anil works T - 5 days, so (T - 5) / 20 + T / 30 = 1. Multiplying by 60 gives 3T - 15 + 2T = 60, so T = 15 days. The 12 days value is the time if both worked throughout. The 14 days value comes from letting Bimal, not Anil, be the one who leaves early. The 18 days value comes from adding 5 idle days to a 13 day estimate.

verification.expr: T = 15; done = (T - 5) / 20 + T / 30; '4' if abs(done - 1) < 1e-9 else '0'

question_text: A sum of Rs 16,000 is lent for one year at 10% per annum. By how much does the interest earned when the rate is compounded half-yearly exceed the interest earned when it is compounded annually?
explanation: Half-yearly, the amount is 16000 x 1.05 x 1.05 = 17640, so interest is 1640, while annual compounding for one year gives just 1600. The excess is Rs 40. The Rs 80 value comes from using 10% per half year instead of 5%. The Rs 20 value comes from halving the correct gap. The Rs 1,640 value is the half-yearly interest itself, not the excess over annual compounding.

question_text: Four boys and three girls are to be seated in a row of seven chairs. In how many ways can they be seated if no two girls sit next to each other?
explanation: Seat the four boys first in 4! = 24 ways, creating five gaps including the two ends. Choose and fill three of those gaps with the three girls in 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 ordered ways, giving 24 x 60 = 1440. The 720 value drops the ordering of the girls by dividing by 3!. The 2880 value comes from allowing six gaps instead of five. The 5040 value is 7!, the count with no restriction at all.

verification.expr: n = factorial(4) * (5 * 4 * 3); '4' if n == 1440 else '0'

question_text: Bag A contains 4 red and 6 green balls, while bag B contains 7 red and 3 green balls. One of the two bags is chosen at random and two balls are drawn from it together. Both drawn balls turn out to be red. What is the probability that bag A was the bag chosen?
explanation: Each bag has 10 balls, so two reds have chance 6/45 from bag A and 21/45 from bag B. Since the bags are equally likely, the required probability is 6 / (6 + 21) = 2/9. The 2/15 value is the unconditional chance of two reds from bag A alone. The 7/9 value is the probability for bag B, the complement. The 1/3 value comes from using 4/10 and 7/10 as single-draw odds and rounding the ratio.

verification.expr: pa = Fraction(comb(4, 2), comb(10, 2)); pb = Fraction(comb(7, 2), comb(10, 2)); post = pa / (pa + pb); '2' if post == Fraction(2, 9) else '0'

question_text: A solid metal cone of base radius 6 cm and height 24 cm is melted down, and 10% of the metal is lost in the process. The remaining metal is recast into solid spheres of radius 2 cm each. What is the largest number of complete spheres that can be made?
explanation: The cone has volume 288 pi cubic cm, and 90% of it is 259.2 pi. Each sphere takes 32 pi / 3 cubic cm, so 259.2 x 3 / 32 = 24.3, and only 24 complete spheres are possible. The 27 value ignores the 10% metal loss. The 25 value comes from rounding 24.3 upward instead of down. The 8 value comes from omitting the factor 1/3 in the volume of a sphere.

verification.expr: cone = 36 * 24 / 3; usable = cone * 0.9; sphere = 4 * 8 / 3; n = int(usable / sphere); '3' if n == 24 else '0'

question_text: Let N be the number whose prime factorisation is 2^5 x 3^4 x 5^2. How many positive divisors of N are perfect squares and are also multiples of 12?
explanation: A divisor 2^a x 3^b x 5^c is a perfect square only when a, b and c are all even, and it is a multiple of 12 only when a is at least 2 and b is at least 1. So a is 2 or 4, b is 2 or 4, and c is 0 or 2, giving 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 divisors. The 12 value allows b = 0 as well, dropping the multiple of 3 condition. The 6 value allows b = 0 but also forces c = 0. The 4 value forgets that c can be 2.

verification.expr: ea = set([0, 2, 4]) & set(range(2, 6)); eb = set([0, 2, 4]) & set(range(1, 5)); ec = set([0, 2]) & set(range(0, 3)); n = len(ea) * len(eb) * len(ec); '2' if n == 8 else '0'

question_text: Three positive numbers are in arithmetic progression. Their sum is 27 and the sum of their squares is 293. What is the product of the three numbers?
explanation: Write the numbers as 9 - d, 9 and 9 + d, since the sum 27 forces the middle term to be 9. Then 243 + 2d squared = 293, so d squared = 25 and the numbers are 4, 9 and 14, whose product is 504. The 729 value comes from taking all three numbers equal to 9, which fits the sum but not the square sum. The 585 value uses d = 4 and the 405 value uses d = 6, neither of which gives 293.

question_text: A non-zero real number x satisfies x + 1/x = 3. What is the value of x^5 + 1/x^5 ?
explanation: Write s(n) = x^n + 1/x^n. Multiplying s(n) by (x + 1/x) gives s(n+1) + s(n-1), so s(n+1) = 3 s(n) - s(n-1) with s(0) = 2 and s(1) = 3. This gives s(2) = 7, s(3) = 18, s(4) = 47 and s(5) = 123. The value 243 comes from assuming the answer is 3^5, that is from treating x + 1/x as if it were x itself. The value 126 is the product 7 times 18, an invented shortcut s(2) times s(3). The value 141 follows from the slip s(4) = 3 times 18 - 3 = 51 and then 3 times 51 - 18.

question_text: If a and b are positive real numbers with a + b = 10, what is the maximum possible value of a^2 b^3 ?
explanation: Split the sum as a/2 + a/2 + b/3 + b/3 + b/3, five positive terms adding to 10. By AM-GM the product (a^2 b^3)/108 is largest when all five terms are equal, so a/2 = b/3 = 2, giving a = 4 and b = 6. Then a^2 b^3 = 16 times 216 = 3456. The value 3125 comes from setting a = b = 5, which maximises only symmetric products. The value 4000 comes from the guess a = 2, b = 8 followed by 4 times 1000. The value 3087 corresponds to a = 3 and b = 7, a nearby but smaller choice.

question_text: The equation (log_3 x)^2 + 3 = log_3 (x^4) holds for exactly two positive values of x. What is the sum of these two values?
explanation: Put t = log_3 x. Since log_3 (x^4) = 4t, the equation becomes t^2 - 4t + 3 = 0, so t = 1 or t = 3, giving x = 3 and x = 27, whose sum is 30. The value 84 comes from misreading the roots as t = 1 and t = 4, which gives 3 + 81. The value 12 comes from adding the roots 1 and 3 after cubing only one of them, that is 9 + 3. The value 28 comes from dropping the constant 3 and using t = 0 and t = 3, so 1 + 27.

question_text: In the coordinate plane, A = (0, 2) and B = (12, 3). A point P moves along the x-axis. What is the smallest possible value of PA + PB ?
explanation: Reflect A in the x-axis to get A' = (0, -2). For any P on the axis PA = PA', so PA + PB equals PA' + PB, which is least when P lies on the segment A'B. The minimum is the length A'B = sqrt(12^2 + 5^2) = 13, reached at P = (4.8, 0). The value 17 comes from adding the two heights and the horizontal gap, 2 + 3 + 12. The value 12 is only the horizontal gap between A and B. The value 15 comes from subtracting the heights instead of adding them and then rounding sqrt(12^2 + 1^2) upward.

verification.expr: import math; d = math.sqrt(12**2 + 5**2); ab = math.sqrt(12**2 + 1**2); '1' if abs(d - 13) < 1e-9 and d > ab else '0'

question_text: Among 200 students, 120 play cricket, 90 play football and 70 play tennis. Exactly 40 play both cricket and football, 30 play both football and tennis, 35 play both cricket and tennis, and 15 play all three games. How many students play exactly one of the three games?
explanation: By inclusion and exclusion the number playing at least one game is 120 + 90 + 70 - 40 - 30 - 35 + 15 = 190. The pairwise counts include the 15 triple players, so the numbers playing exactly two games are 40 - 15 = 25, 30 - 15 = 15 and 35 - 15 = 20, a total of 60. Subtracting the 60 and the 15 from 190 leaves 115 who play exactly one game. The value 130 comes from subtracting only 60 and forgetting the triple group. The value 100 comes from subtracting 2 times 15 twice over. The value 145 treats the pairwise figures as exactly-two counts already.

verification.expr: union = 120 + 90 + 70 - 40 - 30 - 35 + 15; exactly2 = (40 - 15) + (30 - 15) + (35 - 15); exactly1 = union - exactly2 - 15; '2' if union == 190 and exactly2 == 60 and exactly1 == 115 else '0'

explanation: Each term splits as 2/((2k-1)(2k+1)) = 1/(2k-1) - 1/(2k+1), so consecutive parts cancel. With the last denominator pair being 47 and 49, k runs from 1 to 24 and the sum collapses to 1 - 1/49 = 48/49. The value 24/49 comes from halving the telescoped result, that is from keeping the factor 1/2 that the numerator 2 has already cancelled. The value 47/49 comes from stopping the cancellation one term early at 1 - 2/49. The value 24/25 comes from miscounting the terms and telescoping to 1 - 1/25.

verification.expr: from fractions import Fraction; part = Fraction(2, 1*3) + Fraction(2, 3*5) + Fraction(2, 5*7); total = Fraction(1) - Fraction(1, 49); '2' if part == Fraction(1) - Fraction(1, 7) and total == Fraction(48, 49) else '0'

question_text: What is the sum of all the odd positive factors of 1800? Type your answer as an integer.
explanation: 1800 factorises as 2^3 x 3^2 x 5^2. An odd factor uses no power of 2, so the odd factors are exactly the factors of 3^2 x 5^2 = 225. Their sum is (1 + 3 + 9)(1 + 5 + 25) = 13 x 31 = 403. Using the full factor sum (1 + 2 + 4 + 8)(13)(31) = 6045 wrongly keeps the even factors, and 13 x 31 miscounted as 12 x 30 = 360 comes from dropping the term 1 in each bracket.

question_text: In a colony of 120 households, every household subscribes to at least one of three newspapers A, B and C. Exactly 70 subscribe to A, 60 subscribe to B and 50 subscribe to C, while 12 households subscribe to all three. How many households subscribe to exactly two of the three newspapers? Type your answer as an integer.
explanation: By inclusion and exclusion, 120 = 70 + 60 + 50 minus (sum of the three pairwise overlaps) plus 12, so the pairwise overlap total is 180 + 12 - 120 = 72. Each pairwise overlap counts the 12 all-three households once, so the exactly-two count is 72 - 3 x 12 = 36. Answering 72 stops at the raw pairwise total, and 48 comes from subtracting 12 only once instead of three times.

question_text: What is the remainder when 3^2024 + 4^2024 is divided by 100? Type your answer as an integer.
explanation: The last two digits of powers of 3 repeat with period 20, and 2024 leaves remainder 4 on division by 20, so 3^2024 ends in the same two digits as 3^4 = 81. The last two digits of powers of 4 repeat with period 10 from the first power onward, and 2024 leaves remainder 4 on division by 10, so 4^2024 ends like 4^4 = 256, that is 56. Then 81 + 56 = 137, whose remainder on division by 100 is 37. Answering 137 forgets the final reduction, and 97 comes from using a period of 4 for powers of 4 and getting 16.

question_text: The positive integers x and y satisfy x + y = 30. What is the largest possible value of x^2 y? Type your answer as an integer.
explanation: Write the product as (x/2)(x/2)y, three quantities whose sum is x + y = 30 and hence fixed. The product of such quantities is largest when they are equal, giving x/2 = y, so x = 20 and y = 10, and the value is 400 x 10 = 4000. Checking the integer neighbours confirms it, since 19^2 x 11 = 3971 and 21^2 x 9 = 3969. Answering 3375 comes from wrongly setting x = y = 15, and 8100 comes from maximising x^2 alone at x = 27.

verification.expr: best=max([x*x*(30-x) for x in range(1,30)]); '4000' if best==4000 else '0'

question_text: In how many distinct arrangements of all eleven letters of the word MISSISSIPPI do no two letters S stand next to each other? Type your answer as an integer.
explanation: Set the four letters S aside and arrange the remaining seven letters M, I, I, I, I, P, P, which can be done in 7!/(4! x 2!) = 105 ways. Those seven letters create eight gaps, and choosing four of them for the four identical letters S keeps every pair of S separated, giving C(8,4) = 70 choices. The count is 105 x 70 = 7350. Answering 34650 is the total number of arrangements with no separation condition, and 8400 comes from using C(8,4) with 120 instead of 105 for the non-S block.

verification.expr: n=(factorial(7)//(factorial(4)*factorial(2)))*comb(8,4); '7350' if n==7350 else '0'

question_text: A trader marks his goods 60% above cost price and then allows two successive discounts of 25% and 20% on the marked price. What is his overall profit or loss percentage?
explanation: Take cost 100, so marked price is 160. After 25% off it is 120, and after a further 20% off it is 96. Selling at 96 against cost 100 is a 4% loss. The 4% profit trap forgets one discount, and the 6% figure comes from misapplying the second discount to cost.

verification.expr: sp=160*0.75*0.8; loss=100-sp; '1' if round(loss)==4 else '0'

question_text: A invests Rs 16000 for 9 months, B invests Rs 24000 for 4 months and C invests Rs 12000 for 10 months in a business. If the total annual profit is Rs 9000, what is B's share?
explanation: Capital-months are 144000, 96000 and 120000, which reduce to the ratio 6:4:5 summing to 15 parts. B holds 4 parts, so B earns 9000 times 4 over 15, equal to Rs 2400. The Rs 3000 trap splits equally, and Rs 3600 uses the wrong part count.

question_text: A vessel holds 60 litres of a milk and water mixture in which milk and water are in the ratio 5:1. How much water must be added so that the ratio of milk to water becomes 5:2?
explanation: The 60 litres contain 50 litres milk and 10 litres water. Milk stays fixed at 50, and for a 5:2 ratio the water needed is 50 times 2 over 5, which is 20 litres. Since 10 litres are already present, 10 more must be added. The 20 figure forgets the existing water.

verification.expr: milk=50; water=10; need=milk*2/5; add=need-water; '2' if add==10 else '0'

question_text: A boat covers 36 km downstream in 2 hours and the same 36 km upstream in 3 hours. What is the speed of the stream?
explanation: Downstream speed is 36 over 2, that is 18 km/h, and upstream speed is 36 over 3, that is 12 km/h. Stream speed is half the difference, so it equals half of 6, which is 3 km/h. The 15 value wrongly reports boat speed, and 6 forgets to halve the difference.

verification.expr: down=36/2; up=36/3; stream=(down-up)/2; '2' if stream==3 else '0'

question_text: A can finish a piece of work in 8 days and B can finish the same work in 12 days. They work on alternate days with A starting on the first day. In how many days will the work be completed?
explanation: With 24 total units, A does 3 units per day and B does 2 units per day. Over 9 alternating days starting with A the completed work is 23 units. One unit remains for B, who needs half a day at 2 units per day, giving 9.5 days in all. The 10 trap rounds up the final partial day.

verification.expr: w=24; a=3; b=2; pairs=w//(a+b); done=pairs*(a+b); days=pairs*2; days=days+1; done=done+a; extra=(w-done)/b; '1' if days+extra==9.5 else '0'

question_text: A sum of Rs 8000 is invested at 20% per annum compounded half-yearly for one year. What is the compound interest earned?
explanation: Half-yearly the rate is 10% over two periods, so the amount is 8000 times 1.1 squared, that is 9680. The interest is 9680 minus 8000, which is Rs 1680. The Rs 1600 value uses simple interest, and Rs 1764 wrongly applies a 20% rate for two full periods.

question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word PENCIL be arranged so that the two vowels E and I are never together?
explanation: All six distinct letters arrange in 720 ways. Treating the two vowels as one block gives 5 factorial times 2, that is 240 arrangements where they sit together. Subtracting leaves 720 minus 240, which is 480. The 240 value counts the together case instead of the apart case.

verification.expr: from math import factorial; ans=factorial(6)-factorial(5)*2; '1' if ans==480 else '0'

question_text: A bag contains 5 red balls and 4 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that at least one of them is red?
explanation: The complement of at least one red is both balls blue, which has probability 6 over 36, that is 1/6, using choose two from four over choose two from nine. Therefore at least one red is 1 minus 1/6, which is 5/6. The 1/6 value reports the complement, and 5/9 uses a single draw.

verification.expr: from math import comb; p=1-comb(4,2)/comb(9,2); '1' if abs(p-5/6)<1e-9 else '0'

question_text: A solid metallic sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small cones, each having base radius 2 cm and height 3 cm. How many such cones can be made?
explanation: The sphere volume uses four-thirds times radius cubed, giving 288 times pi. Each cone volume uses one-third times base area times height, giving 4 times pi. Dividing 288 by 4 yields 72 cones. The 36 trap uses half the sphere volume, and 108 mishandles the cone factor.

verification.expr: sphere=4/3*6**3; cone=1/3*2**2*3; '1' if round(sphere/cone)==72 else '0'

question_text: What is the remainder when 3 raised to the power 101 is divided by 100?
explanation: Powers of 3 modulo 100 cycle with period 20, since 3 to the power 20 leaves remainder 1. As 101 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 20, the value equals 3 to the power 1 modulo 100, which is 3. The 1 trap forgets the leftover exponent, and 27 uses exponent 3.

question_text: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression is given by 3n squared plus 5n. What is the 12th term of this progression?
explanation: The nth term equals the sum of n terms minus the sum of n minus one terms. Here that difference simplifies to 6n plus 2, so the 12th term is 72 plus 2, which is 74. The 72 trap drops the constant, and 80 mishandles the sum-difference step.

question_text: **If a + b + c = 0 and a² + b² + c² = 14, what is the value of a⁴ + b⁴ + c⁴?**
explanation: With a+b+c=0, we get ab+bc+ca = -(a²+b²+c²)/2 = -7, so (ab+bc+ca)² gives a²b²+b²c²+c²a² = 49 (the abc*sum term vanishes). Then a⁴+b⁴+c⁴ = (a²+b²+c²)² - 2(a²b²+b²c²+c²a²) = 196 - 98 = 98. The 196 value forgets to subtract the cross terms, 49 stops at the cross-term sum, and 72 mishandles the squaring.

question_text: For x > 0, what is the minimum value of x^2 + 250/x?
explanation: Split the second term to apply AM-GM on three parts: x^2 + 125/x + 125/x is at least 3 times the cube root of (x^2 * 125/x * 125/x) = 3 * cube root of 15625 = 3*25 = 75, with equality when x^3 = 125, so x = 5. Splitting into only two equal pieces gives the wrong 100 figure.

verification.expr: f=lambda t: t*t+250/t; '3' if abs(min(f(n/100) for n in range(1,2000))-75)<1e-6 else '0'

question_text: What is the value of the product (log base 2 of 3)(log base 3 of 4)(log base 4 of 5) ... (log base 63 of 64)?
explanation: Writing each factor as ln of the top over ln of the base makes the chain telescope, leaving ln 64 divided by ln 2, which equals log base 2 of 64 = 6 since 2^6 = 64. The 32 trap divides 64 by 2, and 5 miscounts the exponent.

verification.expr: '4' if abs(math.log(64,2)-6)<1e-9 else '0'

question_text: Points A(2, 3) and B(8, 5) lie in the coordinate plane. A point P is chosen on the x-axis. What is the least possible value of AP + PB?
explanation: Reflect A across the x-axis to A'(2, -3); then AP equals A'P, so AP + PB is least when A', P, B are collinear, giving the straight distance A'B = sqrt((8-2)^2 + (5+3)^2) = sqrt(36+64) = 10. Using the direct distance AB gives the sqrt(52) trap.

verification.expr: '4' if abs(math.hypot(8-2,5-(-3))-10)<1e-9 else '0'

question_text: Among 100 employees, 40 use Python, 48 use R, and 45 use SQL. Also 15 use both Python and R, 18 use both R and SQL, 12 use both Python and SQL, and 8 use all three tools. How many employees use exactly one of the three tools?
explanation: The number in at least one is 40+48+45 -15-18-12 +8 = 96. Those in exactly two pairs number (15+18+12) - 3*8 = 21, and 8 use all three, so exactly one is 96 - 21 - 8 = 67. The 96 trap stops at the union total, and 59 subtracts the pairwise counts without adding back the triple.

verification.expr: A,B,C=40,48,45; ab,bc,ac=15,18,12; abc=8; atleast=A+B+C-ab-bc-ac+abc; two=(ab+bc+ac)-3*abc; one=atleast-two-abc; '1' if one==67 else '0'

explanation: Each term 1/((2k-1)(2k+1)) equals one half times (1/(2k-1) - 1/(2k+1)), so the ten terms telescope to one half times (1 - 1/21) = one half times 20/21 = 10/21. Forgetting the factor of one half gives the 20/21 trap.

verification.expr: from fractions import Fraction; s=sum(Fraction(1,(2*k-1)*(2*k+1)) for k in range(1,11)); '2' if s==Fraction(10,21) else '0'

question_text: Find the sum of all positive integer divisors of 360 (including 1 and 360 themselves).
explanation: Write 360 as 2^3 times 3^2 times 5. The sum of divisors is multiplicative, so it equals (1+2+4+8) times (1+3+9) times (1+5), that is 15 times 13 times 6, which is 1170. A common slip is to forget the constant term 1 in one bracket, giving 14 times 13 times 6 or 1092, or to stop at 2^2 and use (1+2+4) which yields 7 times 13 times 6 or 546. The full factorisation gives 1170.

verification.expr: s=sum(d for d in range(1,361) if 360%d==0); '1170' if s==1170 else '0'

question_text: An arithmetic progression has first term 7 and common difference 4. Find the sum of its first 30 terms.
explanation: The sum of the first n terms is (n/2) times (2a + (n-1)d). With a equal to 7, d equal to 4 and n equal to 30, this is 15 times (14 + 29 times 4), that is 15 times (14 + 116), which is 15 times 130, giving 1950. Using (n-1) as 30 instead of 29 gives 15 times 134 or 2010, and forgetting to double a gives 15 times (7 + 116) or 1845. The correct sum is 1950.

verification.expr: s=sum(7+4*k for k in range(30)); '1950' if s==1950 else '0'

question_text: What is the remainder when 17 raised to the power 256 is divided by 100? (In other words, give the last two digits of 17^256.)
explanation: The last two digits of powers of 17 repeat with a cycle length of 20, since 17^20 ends in 01 modulo 100. Reducing the exponent, 256 leaves remainder 16 when divided by 20, so 17^256 has the same last two digits as 17^16. Squaring step by step modulo 100 gives 17^2 as 89, 17^4 as 21, 17^8 as 41, and 17^16 as 81. Treating the cycle length as 4 (as if it were 7) mistakes it, and assuming 256 is a multiple of the period wrongly yields 01. The answer is 81.

question_text: In a group of 200 people, 100 use app A, 90 use app B and 80 use app C. Exactly 40 people use all three apps and exactly 20 people use none of the three. How many people use exactly two of the three apps?
explanation: The number using at least one app is 200 minus 20, that is 180. By inclusion and exclusion, at least one equals the sum of singles minus the sum of the three pairwise overlaps plus the triple overlap, so 180 equals 270 minus (sum of pairwise) plus 40, giving the sum of pairwise overlaps as 130. Each pairwise overlap counts the all-three group as well, so the sum of pairwise overlaps equals (exactly two) plus three times 40. Thus exactly two equals 130 minus 120, which is 10. Forgetting to subtract the triple three times leaves 130, and ignoring the 20 with none gives a different single total. The answer is 10.

verification.expr: pair=270-180+40; exactly2=pair-3*40; '10' if exactly2==10 else '0'

question_text: A positive integer 30 is to be written as a sum of one or more positive integers. Over all such ways, what is the maximum possible value of the product of those parts?
explanation: To maximise the product for a fixed sum, break the number into parts of size 3 as much as possible, avoiding parts of 1, and use a 2 only when the leftover after taking threes is 1 (by combining 3 plus 1 into 2 plus 2). Here 30 is exactly ten 3s with no remainder, so the best product is 3 raised to the power 10, which is 59049. Using all 2s gives 2 raised to the power 15 or 32768, which is smaller, and mixing in a part of 1 only lowers the product. The maximum is 59049.

verification.expr: best=max(3**a*2**b for a in range(11) for b in range(16) if 3*a+2*b==30); '59049' if best==59049 else '0'

stimulus.markdown:
For most of human history, the night sky was a shared inheritance: a band of stars visible to anyone who looked upward. That inheritance is quietly dissolving. The spread of electrified cities has scattered artificial light into the atmosphere, where dust and moisture scatter it further, producing a diffuse glow that astronomers call skyglow. Under this veil, the faint light of distant stars is simply drowned out. Surveys now suggest that a large share of people alive today have never seen the Milky Way from where they live, and that the brightness of the night sky over inhabited regions is rising by a few per cent each year.

The consequences reach well beyond stargazing. Many organisms time their behaviour by natural cycles of darkness. Migrating birds, which navigate partly by the stars, can be disoriented by illuminated buildings; insects exhaust themselves circling lamps; hatchling sea turtles, which instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, may turn inland toward roads instead of out to sea. In each case a cue that was reliable for millions of years has been overwritten by a human signal.

What makes light pollution unusual among environmental problems is how readily it can be reversed. Carbon dioxide lingers in the atmosphere for centuries; a poorly aimed streetlamp stops polluting the moment it is switched off or shielded. Lighting that points downward, that is no brighter than a task requires, and that is dimmed when no one is present can preserve both safety and darkness. The obstacle is not technical but a habit of mind that equates more light with more progress. When a result in science is described as 'replicated,' it means that an independent team, following the same procedure, has obtained a similar finding. Replication is often called the gatekeeper of reliable knowledge, because a single study, however carefully done, can be misled by chance, by an unusual sample, or by an undetected flaw in its design. Only when a result reappears under different hands does the community gain confidence that it reflects something real rather than an accident of one laboratory.

In recent years, however, attempts to repeat well-known studies have frequently failed to reproduce the original effects. Several factors contribute. Researchers face strong incentives to publish striking, novel results, while careful repetitions of someone else's work attract little reward and are seldom published. Small samples can yield impressive-looking outcomes that vanish when the study is enlarged. And the freedom to analyse data in many ways allows a researcher, even unintentionally, to keep adjusting the analysis until a pattern emerges.

None of this means that science is broken. The very fact that the failures are being documented is itself a product of the scientific method turning its scrutiny on its own practices. Reforms are already spreading: some journals now invite researchers to register their hypotheses and planned analyses before collecting data, and commit to publishing the results whether or not they are striking. Others reserve space specifically for replication studies. What looks at first like a crisis of confidence may be better understood as a discipline learning, in public, to hold itself to its own standards.

A city map is never a perfect copy of the city it represents. If it were, it would have to be exactly as large and as complicated as the city itself, and so would be useless to a traveller. The value of a map lies precisely in what it leaves out. By dropping countless details and keeping only roads, rivers, and a few landmarks, a map becomes small enough to hold in the hand and clear enough to guide a journey.

The same principle applies to scientific models. A model of the weather, or of a population of animals, does not try to capture every raindrop or every individual creature. Instead it keeps the features that matter for the question being asked and ignores the rest. A model built to predict tomorrow's temperature can safely leave out the colour of people's umbrellas; a model of how a disease spreads can ignore the brand of car that infected people drive. Choosing what to leave out is not a weakness of a model but the very thing that makes it useful.

This has a practical lesson. When we judge a model, the right question is not 'Is it complete?' but 'Is it useful for its purpose?' A simple model that answers the question at hand may be far more valuable than an elaborate one that tries to include everything and so becomes impossible to understand. As one saying among scientists puts it, all models are wrong, but some are useful. Wisdom lies in matching the simplicity of the model to the job it must do.

Before the middle of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, setting clocks by the moment the sun stood highest overhead. A traveller moving west by carriage might find each new town a few minutes behind the last, and nobody minded, because journeys were slow enough that small differences never mattered. Railways changed that arithmetic. A train that left one city at noon and reached another whose clocks also read noon had, on paper, taken no time at all. Timetables became puzzles, and collisions on single-track lines were a real danger when two crews disagreed about when a siding had to be cleared.

The response was not a government decree but a private one. Railway companies began publishing schedules based on a single reference clock, usually the time kept at their largest terminus, and asked stations along the line to follow it. Towns that resisted found themselves consulting two clocks: one on the church tower for daily life and one at the station for departures. In practice the station clock won, because it governed the arrival of mail, freight and visitors.

Only later did legislatures ratify what commerce had already settled, dividing territories into broad zones within which every clock agreed. The reform is often described as a triumph of science, and astronomers did supply the measurements, but the pressure came from the ledger rather than the observatory. What made local time intolerable was not that it was inaccurate; by the standard of the sun it was perfectly accurate. It was that accuracy of that kind could not be shared. A network needs its members to agree on a convention, and the value of the convention lies almost entirely in the agreement, not in the truth of the thing agreed. That is why the change, once begun, spread quickly: each town that joined made joining more attractive for the rest.
