**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

Beneath the floor of most forests lies a dense mesh of fungal threads, thinner than hair and far more numerous than roots. Many of these fungi wrap themselves around, or grow into, the roots of trees. It is an organism with interests of its own, and it may retain much of what passes through, trading resources on terms that favour itself rather than any particular tree.

None of this makes the network unimportant. A seedling that gains even a modest supply of minerals in its first seasons may survive a drought it would otherwise not survive, and that is a large effect from a small transfer. **Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

For much of the twentieth century, planners in growing cities treated the bicycle as a relic. Streets were widened, parking was added, and the space left for anyone on two wheels shrank to a painted strip beside fast traffic. Cycling did not disappear, but it became a choice for the brave.

In the last three decades many of those same cities have reversed course. The reason is mostly arithmetic. A lane of road carries far more people per hour on bicycles than in cars, because a bicycle needs about a tenth of the space and, when parked, almost none. Cities that could not afford to widen a single street found they could move more residents simply by changing what the existing width was used for.

Comfort turned out to matter more than exhortation. Where a city merely painted lines on the asphalt, ridership rose a little. Where it separated the cycle lane from moving traffic with a kerb or a row of parked cars, ridership rose sharply, and the new riders included many more children and older people. Surveys give a consistent explanation: most people are willing to cycle but unwilling to cycle beside lorries.

The change has limits. Bicycles work best for trips under about eight kilometres, so a city spread thinly over a wide area will always need other options, and hills and heavy rain reduce the numbers. Freight and emergency vehicles still need road space. What the experience of recent decades suggests is narrower than a slogan: for short journeys in dense districts, the cheapest way to add capacity is often to give a little room to bicycles, and the room only works if it feels safe.

For centuries, cartographers left blank the interiors of continents they had not surveyed, and some filled the emptiness with drawings of imagined beasts. These flourishes were not mere decoration. A map is a claim about what is worth recording, and the choice of what to include always reflects the purposes of those who commission it. A trade map emphasises ports, rivers, and the shortest routes between markets; a military map foregrounds ridges, passes, and the width of fords. Neither is a neutral mirror of the land, because no map can show everything at once. To be useful, a map must leave things out.

This selective quality is precisely what makes maps powerful and, at times, misleading. A traveller who trusts a road map assumes that the roads shown are the ones that matter, and rarely wonders about the villages the mapmaker chose to omit. When an authority draws a boundary as a firm line, the line can come to feel as solid as a wall, even where the ground itself offers no such division. In this way a map does not simply describe a territory; it quietly shapes how people imagine and argue about that territory.

Modern digital maps intensify the effect rather than dissolving it. They appear complete and objective, yet every one rests on decisions about which streets to label, which businesses to display, and which neighbourhoods to render in detail. The reader sees a clean surface and forgets the editing beneath it. Understanding a map, then, requires more than reading its symbols. It requires asking who made it, for whom, and what they had reason to leave in the blank spaces.

A trade map emphasises ports, rivers, and the shortest routes between markets; a military map foregrounds ridges, passes, and the width of fords. Neither is a neutral mirror of the land, because no map can show everything at once. To be useful, a map must leave things out.

They appear complete and objective, yet every one rests on decisions about which streets to label, which businesses to display, and which neighbourhoods to render in detail. The reader sees a clean surface and forgets the editing beneath it. Understanding a map, then, requires more than reading its symbols. stimulus.markdown:
When a forest burns, the loss looks total. Yet many woodlands have evolved not merely to survive fire but to depend on it. The cones of certain pines are sealed shut with resin and open only when the heat of a blaze melts that seal, releasing seeds onto ground newly cleared of competitors and enriched with ash. For such trees, a fire is not a disaster but the signal to reproduce. Ecologists describe these systems as fire-adapted, and they are far more common than the popular image of fire as pure destruction suggests.

The difficulty is that not all fires are alike. A frequent, low-intensity fire clears undergrowth while leaving mature trees standing, and many species are tuned to exactly this rhythm. When people suppress every small fire in order to protect property, dead wood and dry brush accumulate year after year. The next fire, when it finally comes, burns hotter and higher than anything the forest is built to withstand, killing even the trees that would ordinarily endure. In trying to prevent fire altogether, a policy can make the eventual blaze far more severe.

This paradox has forced a rethinking of how forests are managed. In several regions, foresters now set controlled burns on purpose, choosing cool, damp days when a fire can be kept small and contained. The aim is not to eliminate fire but to restore its natural frequency, so that fuel never builds to dangerous levels. The approach demands patience and public trust, since a deliberate fire is an unsettling sight. But it reflects a hard lesson: a landscape shaped by fire cannot be kept safe by pretending fire away.

options.1: Foresters in several regions have recently begun to distrust the public's reaction to any deliberate fire.
options.2: Because many forests are adapted to regular fire, suppressing all fires can make later blazes more destructive.
options.3: The resin-sealed cones of certain pines will open only when a passing blaze first melts the seal and then frees the seeds.
options.4: Controlled burns should be set on damp days so that the flames stay small, contained, and easy to watch.

explanation: The passage builds from fire-adapted forests to the paradox that blanket suppression lets fuel accumulate and produces worse fires, which the correct option summarises. The damp-day detail and the pine cones are supporting examples, and public distrust is a practical hurdle mentioned in passing, not the core claim.

The public library began as a simple idea: that useful books should be available to anyone, not only to those who could afford to buy them. Early lending libraries charged a small fee, which kept out the very readers who might have gained the most. The breakthrough came when towns agreed to pay for libraries out of shared taxes, so that borrowing became free at the point of use. A reader needed only to live in the town and to return the books on time. For many families, the library was the first place where knowledge cost nothing.

Over time, libraries grew into something larger than shelves of books. They became quiet places to study, warm rooms to sit in, and centres where people could ask a trained librarian for help finding what they needed. Children attended reading hours, job seekers used the desks, and newcomers to a town found notices about local life. The building offered not just texts but a shared space open to all, regardless of wealth.

Today, when a great deal of information sits a click away, some people ask whether libraries are still needed. Yet the answer many communities give is yes. Not everyone owns a computer or a quiet place to work, and not every question is easily answered by a search engine. The library remains what it has long been: a place where help and knowledge are offered freely, to whoever walks through the door.

question_text: **Which of the following best captures the main point of the passage?**

options.1: Librarians spend more of their time helping job seekers than assisting young children.
options.2: The public library has long offered free access to knowledge and remains valuable today.
options.3: Early lending libraries failed mainly because the fees they charged were set far too high.
options.4: Search engines have replaced most of the services that public libraries once provided.

explanation: The passage traces the library from free tax-funded lending to a broad community space and argues it is still needed, which the correct option captures. The fee point is background, the search-engine claim is the view the passage rejects, and the comparison of job seekers to children is never made.

Five sentences are given below. Four of them can be joined to form a coherent paragraph on a single idea, while one does not fit.

(1) Honeybees communicate the location of food through a series of movements known as the waggle dance.
(2) The angle of the dance relative to vertical tells other bees the direction of the flowers.
(3) The duration of each waggle run signals roughly how far away the food source lies.
(4) A large hive can hold tens of thousands of individual worker bees during summer.
(5) Observers can even estimate distance by timing how long each run lasts.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 all describe how the waggle dance encodes the direction and distance of food, forming one connected idea. Sentence 4 shifts to hive population, an unrelated statistic that breaks the theme, so it is the misfit. The other options each belong to the dance-communication chain.

(3) Wider access to printed texts helped standardise spelling across many regions.
(4) Lower prices meant that ideas spread far beyond wealthy monasteries and courts.
(5) Many early manuscripts were decorated with gold leaf and elaborate hand-painted borders.

**Which sentence is the odd one out?**
explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 4 all trace the effects of printing, faster output, standard spelling and cheaper wider access, so they cohere. (3) When water grows too warm, the corals expel these algae and turn a pale white.
(4) A prolonged loss of algae can leave the corals starving and eventually dead.
(5) Deep-sea trenches remain among the least explored regions of the entire planet.

explanation: Sentences 1 to 4 build one picture of coral reefs and their reliance on algae, including the bleaching that follows warming. The four sentences below, labelled 1 to 4, form a paragraph when placed in the correct order. Rearrange them into the most logical sequence.

2. Within a few summers, shaded pavements were measurably cooler than bare ones.
3. Residents also reported walking more often once the routes felt pleasant.
4. The idea began as a simple response to rising temperatures in the centre.

**Select the correct order.**
explanation: Sentence 4 opens with the origin of the idea, sentence 1 states the action taken, sentence 2 gives the first measured result, and sentence 3 adds a further outcome. The order 4-1-2-3 moves from motive to action to results. Sequences starting with 1 skip the framing motive, and 4-2-1-3 places a result before the action that caused it.

3. Without it, the same surface would swing between scorching days and freezing nights.
4. On our world that blanket is mostly nitrogen with a smaller share of oxygen.

**Select the correct order.**
explanation: Sentence 2 defines the atmosphere, sentence 4 names its main gases, sentence 1 explains the warming effect of that layer, and sentence 3 states the consequence of its absence. The order 2-4-1-3 flows from definition to composition to function to contrast. 3. Only then did the owner adjust the heat to bring out the flavour.
4. Uneven beans, she knew, would scorch and cook at different rates.
